propositions.text: Ms. Tshimuangi seeks judicial review of the RAD decision dismissing her appeal and confirming the RPD decision.
propositions.quote: Tshibola Marguerite Tshimuangi, a citizen of the Democratic Republic of the Congo [DRC] and permanent resident of South Africa, is seeking judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Appeal Division [RAD], dated January 12, 2023 [Decision], in which the RAD dismissed Ms. Tshimuangi’s appeal and confirmed the decision of the Refugee Protection Division [RPD].

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Tshimuangi seeks judicial review of the RAD decision dismissing her appeal and confirming the RPD decision, court states.

propositions.text: RAD found Ms. Tshimuangi is referred to in Article 1E of the Refugee Convention and is neither a refugee nor in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The RAD confirmed that Ms. Tshimuangi is a person referred to in Article 1E of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, 28 July 1951, 189 UNTS 137 [Convention], and that she is neither a refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found Ms. Tshimuangi is excluded under Article 1E and not a refugee or protected person, earlier decision-maker finds.

propositions.text: Ms. Tshimuangi does not dispute South African permanent residents have rights like citizens.
propositions.quote: Before the Court, and as she confirmed at the hearing of this application, Ms. Tshimuangi is not disputing the fact that permanent residents of South Africa have essentially the same rights as citizens of this country.

propositions.text: RAD erred by analyzing fear of persecution after concluding Article 1E applies and in its analysis of fear in South Africa.
propositions.quote: Ms. Tshimuangi contends, however, that the RAD erred fatally (1) in the fact that it analyzed Ms. Tshimuangi’s allegations of fear of persecution in South Africa after concluding that she was referred to in section E of Article 1 of the Convention [Article 1E of the Convention]; and (2) in its analysis of the alleged fear of persecution in South Africa.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Tshimuangi accepts South African permanent residents have citizen-like rights but argues RAD erred in analyzing fear after Article 1E exclusion and in that analysis, applicant argues.

propositions.text: Ms. Tshimuangi asks the Court to set aside RAD decision and refer case to a different panel for reconsideration.
propositions.quote: Ms. Tshimuangi is therefore asking the Court to set aside the RAD’s decision and to refer the case back to a differently constituted panel for reconsideration.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Tshimuangi requests the Court to set aside RAD decision and refer case to a new panel, applicant requests.

propositions.text: Minister says application should be dismissed as RAD's exclusion under Article 1E is reasonable.
propositions.quote: The respondent, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration [the Minister], replies that the application for leave and judicial review should be dismissed since the exclusion found by the RAD under Article 1E of the Convention is essentially reasonable.

propositions.text: Minister argues RAD analyzed fear of South Africa before excluding under section 98, contrary to RPD.
propositions.quote: The Minister submits that (1) contrary to the RPD, the RAD analyzed Ms. Tshimuangi’s alleged fear of South Africa, her country of residence, before excluding her under section 98 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 7 [Immigration Act];

propositions.text: Minister says RAD reasonably analyzed fear of South Africa to determine Article 1E referral and exclusion under section 98, meeting Convention objectives.
propositions.quote: (2) it was reasonable for the RAD to analyze Ms. Tshimuangi’s alleged fear of South Africa, her country of residence, in order to determine whether or not she was referred to in Article 1E of the Convention and excluded under section 98 of the Immigration Act, since this meets the objectives of the Convention;

propositions.text: Minister argues RAD's analysis of fear was reasonable and timing of that analysis does not affect reasonableness of decision.
propositions.quote: (3) in any event, the analysis of Ms. Tshimuangi’s alleged fear of persecution in South Africa was reasonable and whether the RAD considered it before or after excluding her does not change the reasonableness of its Decision.

paragraphs.summary: Minister argues RAD's exclusion under Article 1E is reasonable, RAD reasonably analyzed fear before exclusion, and timing does not affect reasonableness, respondent argues.

propositions.text: Court will allow Ms. Tshimuangi’s application for judicial review.
propositions.quote: For the following reasons, Ms. Tshimuangi’s application for judicial review will be allowed.

paragraphs.summary: Court allows Ms. Tshimuangi's application for judicial review, court concludes.

propositions.text: Parties agree section 98 does not permit considering fear of country of residence after Article 1E referral and exclusion under section 98.
propositions.quote: The parties confirmed that section 98 of the Immigration Act does not permit consideration of a claimant’s allegations of fear of his or her country of residence after it has been determined that said claimant is referred to in Article 1E of the Convention and therefore excluded under section 98 of the Immigration Act.

paragraphs.summary: Parties agree section 98 forbids considering fear of country of residence after Article 1E referral and exclusion, court states.

propositions.text: Parties agree sections 96 and 97 apply only to country of nationality, not country of residence.
propositions.quote: The parties also confirmed that the Immigration Act does not allow a claimant’s allegations of fear of his or her country of residence to be examined under the aegis of sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration Act since these sections only apply to a person’s country of nationality (if the person has one).

paragraphs.summary: Parties agree sections 96 and 97 apply only to country of nationality, not residence, court states.

propositions.text: RAD examined fear of South Africa after concluding Article 1E referral and exclusion under section 98, contrary to section 98 wording.
propositions.quote: However, the RAD, which confirmed the RPD’s decision without reservation, examined Ms. Tshimuangi’s alleged fear of South Africa after concluding that Ms. Tshimuangi was referred to in Article 1E of the Convention and excluding her under section 98 of the Immigration Act. This is contrary to the clear wording of section 98 of the Immigration Act.

paragraphs.summary: RAD examined fear of South Africa after Article 1E referral and exclusion, contrary to section 98, court finds.

propositions.text: RAD relied on section 97 to analyze fear of country of residence, contrary to section 97 wording applying only to nationality.
propositions.quote: Moreover, since the RAD confirmed the RPD’s analysis without reservation, there is every indication that it was relying on section 97 of the Immigration Act in analyzing Ms. Tshimuangi’s alleged fear of South Africa, her country of residence. This too is contrary to the clear wording of the Immigration Act since section 97 refers only to Ms. Tshimuangi’s country of nationality, not her country of residence.

paragraphs.summary: RAD relied on section 97 to analyze fear of residence country, contrary to section 97 applying only to nationality, court finds.

propositions.text: RAD's reasoning was erroneous and fundamentally flawed for excluding under Article 1E and then analyzing fear of country of residence relying on section 97.
propositions.quote: Given that the RAD, like the RPD before it, excluded Ms. Tshimuangi under Article 1E of the Convention and section 98 of the Immigration Act, and yet subsequently examined Ms. Tshimuangi’s allegations of fear of South Africa, and given that, in addition, the RAD examined Ms. Tshimuangi’s allegations of fear of her country of residence by relying on section 97 of the Immigration Act, the Court finds that the RAD’s reasoning was erroneous and fundamentally flawed.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD's reasoning erroneous and fundamentally flawed for excluding under Article 1E then analyzing fear of residence relying on section 97.

propositions.text: RAD decision was unreasonable based on erroneous reasoning and cannot be upheld; file returned for reconsideration.
propositions.quote: The RAD’s decision was thus unreasonable as it was based on erroneous reasoning (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 83, 86–87) and, consequently, cannot be upheld. Ms. Tshimuangi’s file will therefore be returned to the RAD for reconsideration.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes RAD decision unreasonable due to erroneous reasoning and returns file for reconsideration.

propositions.text: Parties argued it was reasonable for RAD to analyze fear of country of residence before Article 1E referral and exclusion under section 98.
propositions.quote: As mentioned above, the parties argued at the hearing that it was reasonable for the RAD to analyze Ms. Tshimuangi’s alleged fear of South Africa, her country of residence, beforehand, or in order to determine whether or not she was a person referred to in Article 1E of the Convention and excluded under section 98 of the Immigration Act.

propositions.text: Minister said this approach meets the objectives of the Convention.
propositions.quote: The Minister pointed out that this approach meets the objectives of the Convention.

propositions.text: Court said objectives of Convention are laudable but approach usurps Parliament's role.
propositions.quote: In the course of the discussion, the Court indicated that the objectives of the Convention were not at stake and that they were unquestionably laudable. Rather, the Court noted that the suggested approach usurped the role of Parliament.

paragraphs.summary: Parties argued RAD reasonably analyzed fear before exclusion; Minister said it meets Convention objectives; court said approach usurps Parliament's role.

propositions.text: Court says parties' suggested approach is not determinative but useful to record for RAD's reconsideration.
propositions.quote: In view of the above-mentioned conclusions as to the nature of the RAD’s decision, the approach suggested by the parties is not determinative in this proceeding. It nonetheless seems useful to put down in writing the position presented to the parties at the hearing, and to briefly describe it. The Court is asking the RAD to consider the comments below as part of its reconsideration.

paragraphs.summary: Court says parties' approach is not determinative but useful to record for RAD's reconsideration, court states.

propositions.text: Parties agree section 98 forbids considering fear of country of residence after Article 1E referral and exclusion under section 98.
propositions.quote: As was mentioned earlier, the parties agree that section 98 of the Immigration Act does not permit consideration of a claimant’s allegations of fear of his or her country of residence after it has been determined that said claimant is a person referred to in Article 1E of the Convention and is therefore excluded under section 98 of the Immigration Act.

paragraphs.summary: Parties agree section 98 forbids considering fear of country of residence after Article 1E referral and exclusion, court states.

propositions.text: Parties agree sections 96 and 97 apply only to country of nationality, not country of residence.
propositions.quote: The parties also agree that the Immigration Act does not allow a claimant’s allegations of fear of his or her country of residence to be examined under the aegis of sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration Act since these sections only apply to a person’s country of nationality (if the person has one).

paragraphs.summary: Parties agree sections 96 and 97 apply only to country of nationality, not residence, court states.

propositions.text: Parties say RPD and RAD may consider fear of country of residence before Article 1E referral and exclusion under section 98.
propositions.quote: However, at the hearing, the parties maintained that the RPD and the RAD may consider a claimant’s alleged fear of his or her country of residence before finding that the claimant is a person referred to in Article 1E of the Convention and excluding the claimant under section 98 of the Immigration Act.

propositions.text: Parties rely on RAD Decision MB8-00025 and Court decisions like Lauture to support their position.
propositions.quote: In particular, the parties refer to a decision of the RAD designated as a jurisprudential guide [Decision MB8-00025] as well as to certain decisions of the Court (e.g., Lauture v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 1121 [Lauture]) in order to support their position.

paragraphs.summary: Parties argue RPD and RAD may consider fear of residence before Article 1E referral and exclusion, citing RAD and Court decisions, respondent argues.

propositions.text: Court finds parties' position indefensible as it reads words into clear text and usurps Parliament's role.
propositions.quote: The Court is persuaded that the parties’ position is indefensible in light of the teachings of the Supreme Court of Canada. Indeed, their position consists in interpreting a clear text in the absence of any ambiguity in Parliament’s intention; their position requires reading into the text of Article 1E of the Convention words and concepts not found there, whereas the text as written suffers from no ambiguity whatsoever. Yet, as I noted in Saint Paul v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 493, by reading new wording into the existing text, the RAD, the RPD and the Court would be taking Parliament’s place.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds parties' position indefensible as it reads words into clear text and usurps Parliament's role, court finds.

propositions.text: Courts must interpret statutes by discovering Parliament's intention; clear and unambiguous words require no further construction.
propositions.quote: When the courts are called upon to interpret a statute, their task is to discover the intention of Parliament. When the words used in a statute are clear and unambiguous, no further step is needed to identify the intention of Parliament.

propositions.text: If statute language is clear, it must be construed in ordinary meaning without reference to cases; intention is deduced from language used.
propositions.quote: As Maxwell stated in The Interpretation of Statutes (12th ed. 1969), at pp. 28-29: If there is nothing to modify, alter or qualify the language which the statute contains, it must be construed in the ordinary and natural meaning of the words and sentences. “The safer and more correct course of dealing with a question of construction is to take the words themselves and arrive if possible at their meaning without, in the first instance, reference to cases.” The rule of construction is “to intend the Legislature to have meant what they have actually expressed.” The object of all interpretation is to discover the intention of Parliament, “but the intention of Parliament must be deduced from the language used,” for “it is well accepted that the beliefs and assumptions of those who frame Acts of Parliament cannot make the law.” Where the language is plain and admits of but one meaning, the task of interpretation can hardly be said to arise.

propositions.text: When an Act is clear, no need to interpret it; a simple reading suffices.
propositions.quote: Or, as Professor P. A. Côté succinctly puts it in Interpretation of Legislation in Canada (1984), at p. 2: It is said that when an Act is clear there is no need to interpret it: a simple reading suffices.

paragraphs.summary: Supreme Court and authorities say courts must interpret statutes by Parliament's intention; clear language requires no further construction, court explains.

propositions.text: Section 98 of the Immigration Act is unambiguous and states persons referred to in Article 1E or F are not refugees or persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The wording of section 98 of the Immigration Act is unambiguous, showing no latent ambiguities (Entertainment Software Association v Société canadienne des auteurs, compositeurs et éditeurs de musique, 2020 FCA 100 at para 84) reading as follows: “A person referred to in section E or F of Article 1 of the Refugee Convention is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.”

paragraphs.summary: Section 98 of the Immigration Act is unambiguous that persons referred to in Article 1E or F are not refugees or protected persons, court finds.

propositions.text: Article 1E of the Convention is plain, clear, and unambiguous in its wording.
propositions.quote: The wording of Article 1E of the Convention is equally plain and clear, and unambiguous.

propositions.text: Article 1E excludes persons recognized by competent authorities as having nationality rights and obligations of their country of residence.
propositions.quote: This Convention shall not apply to a person who is recognized by the competent authorities of the country in which he has taken residence as having the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of the nationality of that country.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Article 1E of the Convention is plain, clear, unambiguous, excluding persons recognized as having nationality rights in their residence country.

propositions.text: Neither the Court, RAD, nor RPD have indicated Article 1E or section 98 of the Immigration Act are ambiguous.
propositions.quote: Neither the Court, nor the RAD, nor the RPD have implicitly or explicitly indicated that Article 1E of the Convention and/or section 98 of the Immigration Act are ambiguous.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no indication from itself, RAD, or RPD that Article 1E or section 98 are ambiguous.

propositions.text: Supreme Court of Canada concluded Parliament’s intent for section 98 of the Immigration Act is clear.
propositions.quote: in Febles v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 SCC 68 at paragraphs 66 and 67, the Supreme Court of Canada concluded that Parliament’s intent for section 98 of the Immigration Act is clear.

paragraphs.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada concluded Parliament’s intent for section 98 of the Immigration Act is clear.

propositions.text: The RAD’s Decision MB8-00025 describes a traditional framework analyzing fear before exclusion, but it is inconsistently applied.
propositions.quote: the RAD sets out what it considers to be the consistent or traditional line of case law...the RAD also presents what it describes as a traditional framework...the analysis the RAD describes as traditional has not...been applied traditionally or consistently.

propositions.text: The RAD acknowledges fear has been analyzed either before or after exclusion by the Court.
propositions.quote: the RAD itself acknowledges that the Court has analyzed fear either before or after excluding a claimant

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD’s traditional framework on fear analysis is inconsistently applied and acknowledges fear has been analyzed before or after exclusion.

propositions.text: In Decision MB8-00025, RAD reads into Article 1E a concept not found there without examining ambiguity as required by Supreme Court.
propositions.quote: the RAD reads into the text of Article 1E of the Convention a concept and words not found there without first...examining whether the wording is ambiguous.

propositions.text: Decision MB8-00025 and Jean v Canada show RAD’s analytical framework requires additions to the Convention and Immigration Act texts.
propositions.quote: the analytical framework proposed by the RAD requires a considerable addition to the current texts of the Convention and/or the Immigration Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD reads concepts into Article 1E without ambiguity examination, requiring additions to Convention and Immigration Act texts.

propositions.text: RAD’s analytical framework reads wording into law not present, attempting to fix perceived legislative gaps.
propositions.quote: the RAD proposes an analytical framework that requires not interpreting the law, but rather reading wording into the law that is not there.

propositions.text: RAD justifies framework by highlighting Convention and Act purposes, concluding legislation does not achieve objectives.
propositions.quote: To justify its analytical framework, the RAD highlights the purposes and objectives of the Convention and the Immigration Act, concluding...the legislation as drafted does not achieve those objectives.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD reads wording into law to fix perceived gaps, justifying by Convention and Act purposes it sees as unmet.

propositions.text: Reading concepts not found in statute usurps legislative authority and violates separation of powers.
propositions.quote: reading a concept not found in a statute into that statute usurps legislative authority and is contrary to the separation of powers principle.

propositions.text: Such reading is contrary to Supreme Court teachings as it makes law rather than interprets it.
propositions.quote: It is also contrary to the teachings of the Supreme Court of Canada, since the Court ends up making law, rather than interpreting or applying it.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds reading concepts into statutes usurps legislative authority, violating separation of powers and Supreme Court teachings.

propositions.text: Separation of powers is fundamental; branches must respect their proper roles and not overstep bounds.
propositions.quote: It is fundamental to the working of government as a whole that all these parts play their proper role. It is equally fundamental that no one of them overstep its bounds...

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Supreme Court emphasizing separation of powers and proper role respect among government branches.

propositions.text: RAD found restricting risk consideration to PRRA stage conflicts with Article 1E purposes.
propositions.quote: the RAD clearly posited that restricting to the pre-removal risk assessment [PRRA] stage any consideration of the risk raised by a refugee protection claimant...is inconsistent with the purposes of Article 1E of the Convention.

propositions.text: RAD analyzed 2012 amendments and found no clear parliamentary intent to limit risk consideration to PRRA stage.
propositions.quote: the RAD pointed out that Parliament would have made a clearer statement of its intention had it wished a particular interpretation of the law

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found limiting risk consideration to PRRA stage conflicts with Article 1E and saw no clear parliamentary intent for such limitation.

propositions.text: RAD noted Parliament would have made clearer statement if PRRA-only risk consideration was intended.
propositions.quote: if it had been Parliament’s intention...one would have expected a clearer statement of that intention.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD noted Parliament would have clearly stated if it intended risk consideration only at PRRA stage.

propositions.text: RAD’s approach reads text into Convention and domestic law motivated by dissatisfaction with Article 1E outcomes.
propositions.quote: the RAD’s approach of reading text into the Convention and incorporating into domestic law...is motivated by its finding that the outcome of applying Article 1E of the Convention as it stands is inadequate.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD reads text into law motivated by dissatisfaction with Article 1E application outcomes.

propositions.text: Supreme Court in R v McIntosh held absurd or unjust results do not justify ambiguity or purposive interpretation.
propositions.quote: the Supreme Court of Canada indicated that the fact that a provision leads to absurd or even unjust results does not justify it being considered ambiguous and that, consequently, a purposive interpretation be applied

propositions.text: Courts must enforce clear legislative language even if results are harsh or absurd.
propositions.quote: where, by the use of clear and unequivocal language capable of only one meaning, anything is enacted by the legislature, it must be enforced however harsh or absurd or contrary to common sense the result may be

propositions.text: Absurdity alone does not create ambiguity or justify broad interpretive analysis.
propositions.quote: The fact that a provision gives rise to absurd results is not, in my opinion, sufficient to declare it ambiguous and then embark upon a broad-ranging interpretive analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The Supreme Court held absurd results do not create ambiguity; clear language must be enforced despite harsh outcomes.

propositions.text: If true meaning of text leads to anomalous results, remedy is to seek parliamentary amendment.
propositions.quote: if...the ‘true meaning’ of a text...leads to anomalous results, the remedy under official doctrine is to turn to Parliament to seek an amendment of the text

paragraphs.summary: The court adds that anomalous results require seeking parliamentary amendment, not judicial reinterpretation.

propositions.text: If language is clear and unambiguous, RPD, RAD, or Court must not read terms into statute even if results seem inadequate.
propositions.quote: if the language is clear and unambiguous, it is not up to the RPD, the RAD or the Court to read terms into the text of a statute, even if the application of the statute as drafted could lead to results that may appear inadequate or contrary to its objectives.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes clear language forbids RPD, RAD, or Court from reading terms into statute despite perceived inadequacies.

propositions.text: Court disagrees with Lauture paragraphs 35 and 38 cited by Minister.
propositions.quote: the Court in this case does not agree with the position expressed in paragraphs 35 and 38 of Lauture, which the Minister cited at the hearing.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal confirmed appeal raised serious question but did not answer certified question; debate continues.
propositions.quote: the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed...that it would not answer the certified question. The debate continues therefore since the Federal Court of Appeal has yet to rule on the matter.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with Lauture cited by Minister and notes ongoing debate as Federal Court of Appeal has not ruled.

propositions.text: RAD’s analysis rests on erroneous legal foundation; Decision is unreasonable and judicial review is allowed.
propositions.quote: Considering that the RAD’s analysis...rests on an erroneous legal foundation, the Decision is unreasonable. Accordingly, the Court will allow the application for judicial review of the Decision

propositions.text: Decision is set aside and matter referred back to RAD for redetermination by different panel; no question certified, no costs awarded.
propositions.quote: The applicant’s application for judicial review is allowed. The Refugee Appeal Division’s decision dated January 12, 2023, is set aside. The matter is referred back to the Refugee Appeal Division for redetermination by a differently constituted panel. No question is certified. No costs are awarded.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD’s analysis legally erroneous, sets aside Decision, allows judicial review, and refers matter back to RAD without costs or certified question.
